summary: Describes the administrative steps a network must follow to connect to the global Internet. It covers the kinds of organizations and registries involved and the practical procedures a new network operator should expect. It is an informational guide.

eli5.summary: Joining the Internet is like moving to a new town: you need to register your address and meet the right offices. This guide lists the offices and the forms.

questions: how to connect a network to the internet
what is an autonomous system number
how much address space do i need
subtitle: A practical checklist for networks joining the Internet

tldr.problem: Networks seeking to connect to the global Internet must navigate multiple administrative steps involving address registration, routing databases, domain names, and security procedures.
tldr.mechanism: This guide walks through the hierarchical process: planning your network, requesting address space from your upstream provider or regional registry, registering an autonomous system number if needed, configuring routing, registering domain names, and setting up reverse DNS delegation.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can systematically connect to the Internet and participate in the global infrastructure using proper administrative procedures.

facts.label: Regional Registries
facts.value: ARIN (Americas, Caribbean, Africa), APNIC (Pacific Rim, Asia), RIPE NCC (Europe, Middle East, Africa)

facts.label: CIDR minimum allocation
facts.value: /20 from ARIN (as of February 1999); /19 from APNIC and RIPE NCC

facts.label: ASN requirement
facts.value: Only needed for multi-homed networks with independent routing policies

facts.label: Address justification period
facts.value: 24 months (or 3 months for ISPs in ARIN region)

today: RFC 2901 remains an informational guide that describes the historical administrative infrastructure of the Internet. While the specific procedures and registries have evolved since publication in August 2000, the fundamental principles of hierarchical address allocation and administrative registration remain core to Internet governance through modern organizations like ICANN and the Regional Internet Registries.

sections.title: Getting Ready to Connect
sections.content:
This guide is for system engineers and technical managers planning to connect their network to the Internet. It assumes basic knowledge of networking and provides step-by-step procedures for the administrative tasks required.

The process involves determining your organization type, designating administrative and technical contacts, planning your network topology, and choosing your upstream provider. Before contacting registries or requesting resources, you must set up representative systems and test them with temporary addresses.

Different organizations need different resources: an end user might get addresses from an Internet Service Provider; a larger organization needing to distribute addresses might contact a Regional Internet Registry directly.
sections.eli5: First you need to pick a person to be in charge, draw a picture of your network, and decide who will help you connect.

sections.title: Getting Address Space
sections.content:
Internet Protocol addresses are allocated hierarchically. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) allocates large blocks to three Regional Internet Registries: ARIN (Americas and Africa), APNIC (Asia-Pacific), and RIPE NCC (Europe and Middle East). These registries in turn allocate smaller blocks to Local Internet Registries and ISPs, who allocate to end users.

The first step is to contact your upstream ISP provider with an address allocation request. Regional registries exist as a last resort if your ISP cannot provide addresses. Address requests are evaluated based on documented needs for the next 24 months using Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) boundaries. You should submit detailed network diagrams and topology information to support your request.

For single-homed networks (connected to one ISP), obtaining address space from your upstream ISP is recommended. For multi-homed networks, Regional Internet Registry membership with a /19 or /20 block may be more appropriate to avoid renumbering if you change providers.
sections.eli5: You ask your Internet company for a block of address numbers. These numbers come from a pyramid: the Internet authority gives big blocks to regional registries, who give smaller blocks to your Internet company, who gives them to you.

sections.title: Autonomous Systems and Routing
sections.content:
An Autonomous System Number (ASN) is needed when your routing policy differs from your upstream provider's, which typically means you are multi-homed (connected to more than one ISP). In nearly all cases, single-homed organizations use their provider's ASN instead of obtaining their own.

If you connect to multiple ISPs or public exchange points, you need to register with a routing database to publish your routing policies. Several routing registries exist including the Routing Arbiter Database (RADB), which serves organizations not covered by regional registries. If you announce routes via BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), register with the routing registry closest to your location. The registries are coordinated through the Internet Routing Registry to ensure consistent routing information.

You do not need to register with a routing database if you simply carry default routes to a single upstream ISP, as the ISP typically registers you.
sections.eli5: If you connect to multiple Internet companies, you need a special number (an Autonomous System Number) and you have to tell the Internet about your own routing choices.

sections.title: Domain Names and Reverse DNS
sections.content:
The Domain Name System provides a hierarchy of names for computers. Top-level domains include generic categories like .com, .net, and .org, as well as two-letter country codes like .ca and .fr. IANA directly registers all country-code top-level domains based on ISO 3166 country codes.

To apply for a country-code domain, first verify the domain is available using the whois command. Check that you have an administrative contact in your country and that your name servers are properly configured. If your country's domain is already registered, contact the administrator to register a second-level domain under it.

IN-ADDR.ARPA domains provide reverse DNS lookup, mapping IP addresses back to domain names. This is essential for most network operations and email reliability. You should ask your upstream provider about registering IN-ADDR.ARPA domains, or contact your regional registry if you obtained address space directly from them.
sections.eli5: You pick a name for your network like example.com. You also need to set up reverse addresses so people can figure out what domain owns an IP address.

sections.title: Security and Network Optimization
sections.content:
Regional registries provide security measures to prevent unauthorized changes to database entries. Your contact information provided in database registrations is public. When registering database objects (templates), follow the exact format required by your registry to avoid errors.

For optimizing traffic on your network and addressing advanced infrastructure challenges, organizations can contact CAIDA (Cooperative Association for Internet Data Analysis), which provides neutral frameworks for engineering and maintaining robust global Internet infrastructure.
sections.eli5: The registries have ways to make sure nobody changes your information without permission, but keep in mind your information is public.
